title: When the Cities Rose
subtitle: The Harappan Civilisation: Urbanism, Technology, Exchange and Transformation
abstract: The Harappan Civilisation represents one of the earliest large-scale urban traditions of South Asia. Its archaeological remains extend across a vast geographical zone encompassing parts of present-day Pakistan and northwestern, western and northern India. This article examines the emergence of Harappan urbanism, the development of cities, water management, craft production, agriculture, long-distance exchange, writing, social organisation, ritual evidence and the transformation of the urban system after the Mature Harappan period. It also evaluates major scholarly debates, including the nature of political authority, the interpretation of the Harappan script, the role of climate and river systems, and the question of cultural continuity. The article distinguishes archaeological evidence from interpretation and avoids treating the decline of the major cities as a simple civilisational disappearance.

sections.title: 1. Introduction: The Cities of the Bronze Age
content: Around the middle of the third millennium BCE, large and highly organised settlements appeared across a wide region of South Asia. Archaeologists today refer to this cultural complex principally as the Harappan Civilisation, after Harappa in present-day Punjab, Pakistan. The older expression 'Indus Valley Civilisation' remains widely used, but the archaeological distribution extends far beyond the Indus Valley itself.

The Harappan phenomenon was not confined to a single river valley. Its settlements occupied diverse environments extending from the Indus system toward the Ghaggar-Hakra region, Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Gujarat and the Arabian Sea coast. The geographical breadth of the archaeological record is therefore essential to understanding the civilisation.

The Mature Harappan urban phase is conventionally placed around 2600–1900 BCE, although regional chronologies differ and the processes leading to urbanisation began earlier. The preceding Early Harappan period contains regional cultures and developing settlement networks, while the centuries after approximately 1900 BCE witnessed major changes in settlement size, material culture, trade networks and patterns of urban life.

The Harappan story is consequently not simply the story of a sudden rise followed by a mysterious disappearance. It is a long process of regional interaction, technological development, urbanisation, adaptation and transformation.

sections.title: 2. Terminology, Chronology and the Limits of the Evidence
content: The expression 'Harappan Civilisation' is preferred in much current archaeological writing because the archaeological horizon extends well beyond the Indus basin. 'Indus Civilisation' is also widely used. 'Indus Valley Civilisation' can be misleading when interpreted too literally, because many important settlements lie outside the narrow Indus Valley.

Chronology is reconstructed primarily from stratigraphy, radiocarbon dating, ceramic sequences, artefact typology and regional archaeological correlations. Dates therefore represent approximate chronological frameworks rather than exact historical years.

A useful broad framework distinguishes an Early Harappan period, a Mature Harappan urban period and a Late or Post-Urban Harappan period. These categories are analytical tools. Different regions experienced these phases differently, and there was no single calendar transition occurring simultaneously at every settlement.

This distinction is important because archaeological cultures do not behave like modern political states. A material culture horizon can represent interaction, shared technologies, exchange networks or cultural convergence without proving that every settlement was governed by one central government.

sections.title: 3. The Geography of the Harappan World
content: The geographical extent of Harappan settlement is one of its most striking characteristics. Major archaeological sites are distributed across territories that today fall within both Pakistan and India.

The civilisation occupied markedly different environments: river plains, semi-arid zones, coastal areas, alluvial landscapes, grasslands and regions close to mineral and marine resources. This diversity helps explain why there was no single Harappan economic model.

The distribution of settlements also demonstrates the importance of regional interaction. Agricultural villages, craft centres, urban settlements and coastal communities formed interconnected systems. Raw materials could move over substantial distances, while finished objects and technological practices circulated between communities.
The geographical question is therefore not simply 'Where was the civilisation?' but also 'How were its different regions connected?'

sections.title: 4. Before the Cities: The Long Road to Urbanism
content: Urban Harappan society emerged from a much longer history of settlement and economic development. Early village communities in South Asia experimented with cultivation, animal management, craft production and more permanent forms of settlement thousands of years before the Mature Harappan cities.

The transition to urban society was therefore cumulative. Population growth, agricultural intensification, technological innovation, regional exchange, craft specialisation and increasingly organised settlements created conditions under which larger urban centres could develop.

Archaeological evidence from Early Harappan settlements demonstrates that regional traditions existed before the highly standardised urban system associated with the Mature Harappan period. This is one reason the origin of the civilisation should not be described as an unexplained urban revolution.
The process instead resembles a long period of experimentation in which different communities developed increasingly complex relationships with land, water, resources and one another.

sections.title: 5. The Rise of the Harappan City
content: The Mature Harappan period witnessed the emergence and expansion of large settlements displaying striking degrees of planning and standardisation.

At sites such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Dholavira, excavations reveal streets, residential areas, public structures, drainage systems, wells, craft areas, fortified zones and differentiated architectural spaces.

The use of standardised bricks in many parts of the Harappan world is particularly significant. Standardisation indicates established technical conventions and shared practices extending beyond individual households.

Urban planning also required labour coordination. Constructing walls, drains, reservoirs, streets and large buildings demanded knowledge, materials, planning and cooperation on a scale greater than that of a small village.

Yet the archaeological record does not provide an undisputed Harappan equivalent of the monumental royal inscriptions found in some contemporary Near Eastern civilisations. There are no securely identified palaces accompanied by royal inscriptions that allow archaeologists to reconstruct a named dynasty or central ruler.
This has produced an important scholarly question: how was such extensive coordination achieved?
questions: Did several regional authorities share common institutions?
Were urban systems maintained through local elites and corporate organisations?
How much political integration existed between distant settlements?

sections.title: 6. Mohenjo-daro: An Urban Centre of Exceptional Scale
content: Mohenjo-daro, located in Sindh, is among the most famous Harappan archaeological sites. Its excavated remains reveal a substantial urban settlement characterised by streets, houses, wells, drains and large architectural complexes.

The famous structure commonly known as the Great Bath is one of the most recognisable monuments of the site. Its precise function remains debated, but its construction demonstrates considerable investment in waterproofing, architecture and controlled access.
Domestic architecture also provides important evidence. Houses included bathing areas, drains and courtyards, while numerous wells indicate sophisticated arrangements for obtaining water.

The distribution of such infrastructure challenges simplistic interpretations of early cities as places dominated exclusively by monumental palaces. Harappan urbanism was expressed substantially through infrastructure embedded in the everyday life of the settlement.

sections.title: 7. Dholavira: Engineering in an Arid Landscape
content: Dholavira, located on Khadir Island in Gujarat's Rann of Kachchh, offers one of the clearest examples of how Harappan communities adapted urban planning to a difficult environment.

UNESCO dates occupation at Dholavira broadly from about 3000 to 1500 BCE and describes the site as one of the best-preserved urban settlements of the Harappan period. Its remains include a fortified city, residential areas, ceremonial spaces, workshops, a cemetery and a remarkable system of reservoirs and water-management structures.

Unlike settlements located beside major perennial rivers, Dholavira had to manage seasonal water availability. Its urban system incorporated reservoirs, channels, drains and arrangements for harvesting and controlling runoff.

The importance of Dholavira lies not merely in the existence of individual water tanks. The water system formed part of the city's overall planning. Construction, drainage, storage and urban space were integrated into a broader engineering response to environmental conditions.

UNESCO also records evidence for craft production involving materials such as copper, shell, stone and semi-precious stones, as well as evidence of inter-regional trade extending beyond the Harappan world.

sections.title: 8. Rakhigarhi and the Eastern Reach of Harappan Settlement
content: Rakhigarhi in Haryana is one of the most important Harappan archaeological sites in present-day India. Its significance lies not only in its size but also in its contribution to understanding settlement networks in the eastern part of the Harappan cultural zone.

Excavated evidence from the site includes settlement remains, pottery, craft materials, structural remains and burial evidence. The site demonstrates that important Harappan communities existed well beyond the Indus river system.

Rakhigarhi therefore matters to the wider historiography because it reinforces a fundamental point: the Harappan world was geographically extensive and cannot adequately be understood through a narrow focus on a handful of famous sites in present-day Pakistan.

sections.title: 9. Lothal and the Maritime Dimension
content: Lothal in Gujarat is associated with craft production and maritime-oriented exchange networks. Its archaeological remains include structures interpreted in connection with industrial activity, bead manufacture and trade.
The settlement's location within the Gulf of Khambhat region placed it within an environment suited to interaction with coastal and overseas networks.

Interpretations of individual structures at Lothal have been debated, including the identification of a structure as a dockyard. It is therefore preferable to distinguish the broader evidence for maritime interaction from any single disputed architectural interpretation.

The coastal archaeological record nevertheless establishes that Harappan communities were capable of participating in long-distance exchange linking the subcontinent with wider networks around the Arabian Sea.

sections.title: 10. Water, Survival and Urban Intelligence
content: Water was fundamental to Harappan settlement. The civilisation occupied regions with dramatically different hydrological conditions, from major river systems to semi-arid environments.

Urban centres responded through different combinations of wells, drains, reservoirs, channels and rainwater or runoff management. These adaptations should not be reduced to a single Harappan 'water technology'; regional solutions differed.

Dholavira provides the clearest large-scale example of reservoir-based water management. Mohenjo-daro demonstrates extensive well and drainage infrastructure. Together these sites show that water was not merely a natural resource but an engineering problem that urban communities actively managed.

The broader lesson is significant: Harappan urbanism depended on the ability to maintain infrastructure over time. The archaeological evidence suggests that environmental knowledge was embedded in settlement planning.

sections.title: 11. Craft Production and Technological Expertise
content: Harappan society produced an extraordinary range of objects: pottery, beads, seals, copper and bronze objects, shell ornaments, stone tools, jewellery, terracotta objects and other specialised materials.

Craft production appears to have been organised in multiple forms. Some activities were carried out at household scale, while particular settlements contain evidence suggesting specialised production.
Bead manufacturing is particularly important. Carnelian, agate, steatite and other materials were processed into finished ornaments, many of which entered long-distance exchange networks.
Dholavira has provided particularly important evidence of bead manufacture. UNESCO notes workshops and artefacts made from copper, shell, stone, semi-precious stones, gold, ivory and terracotta.

Technological sophistication should not be judged solely by the presence of monumental buildings. Precision in drilling, polishing, firing, metallurgy and standardisation can represent equally important expressions of technical knowledge.

sections.title: 12. Standardisation, Measurement and Exchange
content: Harappan archaeology is characterised by extensive evidence of standardised weights and measures.

Standardisation is significant because it facilitates exchange and administration. However, the existence of standardised weights does not by itself prove a single central government. Shared measurement systems can spread through commercial institutions, cultural conventions or interconnected regional authorities.

The repeated appearance of comparable weights and artefact forms across widely separated settlements nevertheless suggests that communities participated in systems of substantial interregional interaction.
Measurement was therefore not a minor technical matter. It formed part of the infrastructure of economic life.

sections.title: 13. Agriculture, Food and Rural Foundations
content: Cities cannot exist without dependable food systems. Harappan urbanism depended upon extensive rural landscapes in which crops were cultivated and animals were managed.

Archaeobotanical and faunal evidence demonstrates the use of multiple crops and animal resources. The agricultural economy was not uniform across the entire civilisation. Different ecological zones encouraged different combinations of cereals, millets, pulses and other crops.

This regional diversity is especially important when examining the later transformation of Harappan society. Communities did not experience environmental change in identical ways. Some adapted agricultural strategies, relocated or reorganised their settlement patterns.
The city was therefore only one part of the Harappan economic system. Villages, farms, pastoral communities, craft settlements and urban centres were interconnected.

sections.title: 14. Trade Across the Arabian Sea and Beyond
content: Harappan communities participated in exchange networks extending beyond the immediate subcontinent.

Archaeological evidence connects Harappan material with regions associated with the Persian Gulf, the Oman Peninsula and Mesopotamia. Mesopotamian textual sources refer to a place called Meluhha, which many scholars associate with the Indus region, although the identification and interpretation of these references remain subjects of scholarly discussion.

Dholavira provides archaeological evidence for interregional exchange involving the Oman Peninsula and Mesopotamian regions. Raw materials such as copper, shell and semi-precious stones moved through these networks.
Long-distance trade was not necessarily controlled by one imperial authority. It could have involved merchants, specialist producers, coastal intermediaries and regional political institutions.
The evidence nevertheless establishes that the Harappan world was not isolated. It participated in a wider Bronze Age system of exchange connecting South Asia with regions to its west.

sections.title: 15. The Harappan Script: The Unsolved Problem
content: Among the greatest mysteries of South Asian archaeology is the writing system found on Harappan seals and other objects.
The signs occur on seals, seal impressions, pottery, tablets, metal objects and other artefacts. Many inscriptions are extremely short, which makes linguistic reconstruction difficult.
The script remains undeciphered. The Archaeological Survey of India described the writing in 2025 as an unsolved problem more than a century after its archaeological discovery.

Numerous decipherment proposals have been advanced. These include attempts to associate the signs with known linguistic families and theories concerning the nature of the underlying language. None has achieved general scholarly acceptance.

This uncertainty imposes an important methodological limitation. We cannot currently read Harappan inscriptions and confidently reconstruct the names of rulers, laws, religious texts or administrative records from them.

At the same time, undecipherment should not obscure what the inscriptions demonstrate. The repeated use of signs across many objects shows that the Harappan communities employed a structured system of graphic communication whose precise linguistic character remains unknown.

source.title: Decipherment of Indus Script: Current Status and Way Forward

sections.title: 16. Belief, Ritual and the Problem of Interpretation
content: Harappan archaeology contains many objects that have been interpreted as religious or ritual: seals depicting animals and human or human-like figures, terracotta figurines, unusual structures, burial practices and objects placed with the dead.
However, identifying the religious meaning of an object is considerably more difficult than identifying the object itself.

The famous 'Pashupati' or 'proto-Shiva' interpretation of a horned figure on a seal is one example of a long-standing debate. The figure has been interpreted in several ways, but the identification with a later Hindu deity cannot be treated as an established archaeological fact.
Similarly, fertility interpretations of female figurines have often been proposed, yet figurines may have had multiple functions and meanings.

A responsible history of Bharat must therefore make a distinction between evidence and later cultural interpretation. The possibility of cultural continuity is a legitimate question; it is not evidence by itself.

sections.title: 17. Death, Burial and Memory
content: Burial practices provide another important source of information about Harappan society.
Burial forms vary across the civilisation and over time. Grave goods can include pottery and personal objects, while some locations contain more elaborate structures.
Dholavira is particularly significant because its cemetery contains different forms of memorial structures. UNESCO notes six types of cenotaphs at the site.
Burial evidence can reveal aspects of social practice, identity and attitudes toward death, but it does not automatically reveal the complete religious beliefs of the society that created it.
Archaeology can show patterns in burial practice. Interpreting what those patterns meant to the people themselves remains more difficult.

sections.title: 18. Society, Inequality and Political Authority
content: Harappan settlements clearly contained social differentiation. Houses varied in size and architectural form; some areas contained specialised activities; fortified and elevated zones occur at certain sites.

Dholavira in particular contains differentiated urban sectors, including a fortified Castle, Bailey, Middle Town and Lower Town. UNESCO interprets the configuration as evidence consistent with a socially stratified society.
The difficulty lies in identifying the precise political structure responsible for this differentiation.

Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, where extensive royal inscriptions and monumental royal architecture provide direct evidence for dynastic rulers, Harappan archaeology offers fewer explicit statements of political authority.

Scholarly models range from centralised state systems to more decentralised or corporate forms of governance. The archaeological evidence currently does not justify presenting one model as conclusively proven.
This uncertainty is intellectually valuable. It demonstrates that complex urban civilisation does not necessarily have to reproduce the political institutions of another region.

sections.title: 19. Knowledge, Engineering and Observation
content: Harappan achievements reveal practical knowledge of geometry, materials, construction and environmental management.
Standardised bricks, repeated architectural proportions, carefully engineered drains, reservoirs and craft technologies demonstrate accumulated technical knowledge.

It would be misleading to project later Indian mathematical or astronomical texts directly backward onto Harappan society without evidence. The Harappans clearly possessed sophisticated practical knowledge, but the exact conceptual frameworks through which that knowledge was expressed remain largely unknown.

The correct historical approach is therefore to recognise what the archaeological evidence demonstrates while resisting the temptation to assign later intellectual systems to earlier societies without documentary support.

sections.title: 20. The Great Transformation After 1900 BCE
content: One of the most important revisions in Harappan scholarship concerns the old idea of a sudden 'collapse'. The archaeological evidence increasingly supports a more complex process of transformation.

After approximately 1900 BCE, many major urban centres declined in size or changed substantially. Long-distance exchange networks weakened, distinctive urban material culture became less widespread in some regions, and populations became more dispersed.
This did not mean that Harappan people disappeared. Settlements continued, but the pattern of settlement and production changed.
Research has investigated multiple possible factors: changes in rainfall, river behaviour, agricultural strategies, economic networks, resource availability and population movement.

Climate appears to have been important in some regions. Recent palaeoclimate research has emphasised repeated drought and long-term hydroclimatic stress, while archaeological studies also indicate substantial human adaptation.
There is therefore no need to choose mechanically between 'climate' and 'human activity'. Environmental change and human adaptation could interact over centuries.

source.title: Centuries of repeated droughts linked to the Indus Valley Civilisation's decline

sections.title: 21. From Urbanisation to Regionalisation
content: The post-urban period should not be understood merely as cultural decay. In several regions, communities reorganised rather than vanished.
Settlement patterns changed. Populations moved toward areas offering different agricultural or ecological opportunities. Material traditions diversified and regional cultures became more pronounced.

Some technologies and cultural practices persisted, while others changed or disappeared. This is why archaeologists increasingly speak of transformation, regionalisation or de-urbanisation rather than a single catastrophic collapse.
The history of the Harappan world after 1900 BCE is therefore a history of adaptation.

sections.title: 22. Continuity and Change: The Difficult Question
content: The relationship between Harappan civilisation and later South Asian cultures is one of the most discussed subjects in Indian archaeology.

Certain broad elements of material culture, settlement practice, agricultural traditions, craft knowledge and cultural motifs show continuity across time and regions. Other features changed significantly.

The survival of a practice does not automatically prove direct continuity from Harappan society to a later historical community. Cultural transmission can occur through many mechanisms, including migration, interaction, adaptation and independent development.
Equally, the absence of a single uninterrupted urban institution does not mean that every earlier tradition disappeared.

The most defensible position is therefore neither absolute continuity nor absolute rupture. The archaeological record suggests a complicated mixture of persistence, transformation, dispersal and regional innovation.

sections.title: 23. The Harappan Civilisation in the Long History of Bharat
content: The Harappan civilisation occupies a foundational position in the deep history of the Indian subcontinent. Its cities existed many centuries before the Mauryan Empire and long before the historical dynasties familiar from inscriptions and literary traditions.

Yet the Harappan world should not be isolated from the broader civilisational history of Bharat. The archaeological record demonstrates that people in the subcontinent had already developed agriculture, settlement networks, craft specialisation, trade systems, engineering traditions and large urban communities.
The civilisation also demonstrates that the subcontinent was connected to the wider Bronze Age world while retaining distinctive regional characteristics.

The later history of Bharat would involve profound transformations in language, political institutions, religious traditions, economic systems and settlement patterns. Harappan society should therefore be treated as an early chapter in a long civilisational history rather than as an exact blueprint for every later Indian institution.

Its importance does not depend on proving that every later cultural form originated in Harappan society. Its importance rests in the archaeological fact that an extraordinary urban civilisation developed in South Asia thousands of years ago and participated actively in the wider ancient world.

sections.title: 24. Historiography: How Our Understanding Has Changed
content: The interpretation of the Harappan civilisation has changed considerably since the first archaeological discoveries.
Early scholarship often relied heavily on comparisons with Mesopotamia and Egypt and searched for familiar models of kingship, conquest and monumental authority.
Later archaeological research increasingly focused on settlement systems, household archaeology, environmental evidence, craft production, trade, subsistence and regional variation.
Scientific methods including radiocarbon dating, archaeobotany, zooarchaeology, metallurgy, isotope analysis, palaeoclimate reconstruction and ancient DNA have expanded the evidence base.
These methods have also made the picture more complicated. Rather than reducing the civilisation to one grand explanation, modern archaeology increasingly reveals multiple interacting processes.
The lesson for the history of Bharat is important: historical confidence should increase with better evidence, but conclusions should also become more precise about what remains uncertain.

sections.title: 25. What the Evidence Actually Allows Us to Say
content: Established archaeological evidence demonstrates the existence of large settlements, sophisticated craft industries, long-distance exchange, standardised weights, planned architecture, water-management systems, specialised production and a distinctive writing tradition.
The evidence also establishes major changes after the Mature Harappan period, including urban decline, regionalisation and shifts in settlement patterns.

Other questions remain unresolved. We do not securely know the language represented by the script. We do not have a complete list of rulers. We cannot confidently reconstruct the political constitution of the civilisation. The precise meaning of many symbols and figurines remains uncertain.
These limitations should not weaken the historical importance of Harappan civilisation. On the contrary, acknowledging uncertainty allows the archaeological evidence to speak more clearly.
A serious history of Bharat should not manufacture certainty where the evidence does not provide it.

sections.title: 26. What the Harappan World Can Teach the Present
content: The Harappan experience contains lessons that extend beyond archaeology.
First, urban civilisation depends on infrastructure. Water supply, drainage, roads, storage and craft production are foundations of civic life.
Second, environmental adaptation is not optional. Dholavira demonstrates how communities can develop sophisticated responses to severe water constraints.
Third, large civilisations depend upon networks rather than isolated cities. Production, agriculture, trade and resource exchange connect urban centres to wider landscapes.
Fourth, complexity does not guarantee permanence. Even highly organised systems can be transformed when environmental, economic and demographic conditions change.

Finally, the Harappan example cautions against assuming that there is only one model of civilisation. The Bronze Age world contained different paths to urban complexity, and South Asia developed its own distinctive form.

sections.title: 27. Conclusion
content: The Harappan Civilisation was not a brief experiment that simply appeared and vanished. It was the product of centuries of regional development and interaction and, after the Mature Harappan urban period, it underwent equally important processes of transformation and adaptation.

Its cities reveal systematic planning. Its water systems reveal environmental engineering. Its craft industries reveal technical expertise. Its weights and exchange networks reveal economic coordination. Its seals and inscriptions reveal a sophisticated but still undeciphered writing tradition.
Its decline is better understood as a transformation of settlement and economic systems than as the disappearance of an entire population.

For the long history of Bharat, the Harappan world establishes an extraordinary early foundation: South Asia was home to large, technologically capable and internationally connected urban societies during the Bronze Age.

The remaining mysteries are equally important. Who were the Harappans? What languages did they speak? How was political authority organised? What did their symbols mean? How much of their cultural inheritance survived into later societies?
Those questions remain open. Archaeology continues to answer some of them, challenge others and redefine the questions themselves.

finalNote: The Harappan Civilisation should be approached with both intellectual confidence and archaeological discipline. Its achievements are extraordinary enough that they do not require exaggeration. The surviving evidence already demonstrates a technologically capable, economically connected and highly organised Bronze Age society whose history is fundamental to understanding the deep past of Bharat.
